source.title: Measure, Don't Optimize: Forecasting Recovery in LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Zirui Song; Hua-Xing Liu; Xiang Wang; Shuai Li; Xin-Ye Li; Lang Gao; Jing-Hui Zhang; Zheng Lu; Feng-Xian Ji; X. Chang; Xiu-Ying Chen

page_placements.theme: Weight and representation diagnostics that predict relearning vulnerability

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests recovery after unlearning with fine-tuning attacks and relates internal accessibility to recovery. It also tests whether optimizing an internal audit changes later recovery; these are conceptual tests of the claim rather than direct reproductions of the original studies.
record.gate_note: The study reports recovery outcomes under fine-tuning on forgotten-entity question–answer pairs, internal-access measurements, and effects of optimizing J-Access. It also reports qualitative control outcomes for unseen twin entities, matched decoys, and refitting the lens. Values used to select the workspace band and audit settings are not treated as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses a Jacobian-lens audit and pre-registered relearning attacks (fine-tuning on a subset of forgotten TOFU entities, scored on held-out entities) across 398 public unlearned checkpoints. It reports residual access above the retain-only gold model and post-attack revival rates. These bear on B (recovery by fine-tuning) and C (unlearning blocks access rather than deleting), and on whether A holds for deep versus shallow configurations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the authors' first finding: most unlearned models, including behaviorally successful ones, retain internal access above the retain-only gold level. Behavioral forgetting therefore conceals internal access.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces and evaluates a Jacobian-lens audit, tests it prospectively with fine-tuning on a subset of forgotten entities, and trains dedicated J-Access-suppression variants. It does not reproduce one specific original unlearning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery association varies by granularity: knowledge-level J-Access has a stronger pooled within-method correlation than identity-level J-Access; item-level discrimination is near chance. The WD-Train suppression weight changes audit score and post-attack revival.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-attack J-Access does not identify which individual facts revive: item-level AUROC is 0.504–0.555, and adding it to baselines gains +0.0002.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual internal access signals predict checkpoint-level, not item-level, relearning recovery.

record.problems: The text reports many aggregate correlations and table values but does not provide their uncertainty estimates here. The attack study uses a stratified subset of the 398-model audit pool. Several control and robustness outcomes are stated without numerical values. Table 4 reports three random seeds per WD-Train setting but no uncertainty values in the provided text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 also reports method-specific percentages significantly above gold after Holm correction; these eight secondary significance percentages were omitted to keep within the 60-row limit while retaining each method's above-gold rate and median J-Access. Other results were retained.

untested.parts: Whether each attacked checkpoint had near-chance targeted accuracy with retained utility is not established per checkpoint.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data is not tested; only a subset of the forgotten entities is used.
Ablating an activation direction to restore behaviour is not tested.
Prompting, jailbreaks, other languages and in-context attacks are not tested.
No robust counter-method is evaluated. WD-Train is an audit-suppression variant and is not claimed to resist attacks.

missing.what: J-Access, UDS and MU values for the causal-criterion families (e.g. GradDiff deep 0.09/0.97/0.56; GradDiff shallow 0.62/0.34/0.44), which show the deep configurations also keep utility
All eight within-method correlations between access and revival are positive (no per-method values given)
Absolute or excess revival rates for the Test 2 attacked pool are not reported; only correlations are

record.verdict_notes: Row version ids used V1/V2/V3; they have been mapped to A/B/C. Table 4 does not say whether revival is excess over the attacked gold model. The source is an AAAI-format preprint dated 2026–2027, so external verification is not possible. WD-Train is the study's own suppression variant; its revival values are kept as outcomes because they measure recovery after relearning.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines recovery after unlearning, including a behaviorally successful subset, but does not establish for each attack-tested checkpoint that targeted accuracy was near chance while general ability was retained.

The relearning attack uses question–answer pairs from a subset of forgotten entities and evaluates disjoint held-out entities. It does not test unrelated or loosely related examples, or the other recovery attacks in the claim.
It measures residual internal access and compares it with activation-patching deletion depth, but does not test ablating an activation direction to restore behavior.
Low-bit quantization recovery is not tested.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information are not tested.
The study does not test a newer counter-method claiming resistance to the listed attacks.
